text:
I would push back a little on the plan to cancel the application and manage things from abroad, because I'm not sure it will actually make things easier for you.

The biggest waiting period for non-married couples is often before the interview. If you cancel now and reapply while you are in Korea, you'll likely end up in a similar position in the future - travelling to Israel where you will wait for the interview without the ability to work. In fact, you could be in a worse position - as if you don't cancel, you are unlikely to be able to leave if you get permission. 

I'd recommend attending the July 13 appointment. At that appointment, you can ask for a tourist visa (B2) that is valid until your next scheduled appointment, and crucially, also request an intervisa. If they grant both (they technically don't have to give you an intervisa, but it is likely they will given you haven't breached the protocol), you'll have permission to leave Israel and return before your next appointment. This gives you the flexibility to go back to Korea and wait for a while.

If you cancel the appointment you also have a significant entry risk to consider if you want to come back for a visit in the meantime. Your four years of continuous residence in Israel means border control may still question your intentions and suspect you are trying to settle, which could also lead to entry being denied. It could really risk your ability to come back and see your partner. 

To your specific questions:
(1) Go to the July 13 appointment. Don't skip it. I would use it to get a tourist visa and an intervisa as described above, and schedule the next interview appointment.
(2) I would recommend against cancelling the application. But if you are determined to do it, you can do it at the July 13 appointment. Otherwise, your partner could also email your PIBA branch, asking to cancel your application and your upcoming meeting. They should mention that you are still in a relationship. If PIBA does not reply or acknowledge their email, I would recommend that they go and inform PIBA in person. If you just keep the application open it could cause problems.   
(3) Being in Israel past your visa expiry is not ideal, but in practical terms one day is a blip, especially when you have an appointment the very next day. Attending the appointment on July 13 is far more important than leaving on July 12.
(4) Unfortunately, your four years of clean history in Israel won't speed up the partner visa process. It will be treated as a standard application.

One last thing: while there is technically no requirement to have your center of life in Israel before receiving the B1, an extended period of separation could raise some questions. However, I think you may have a reasonable explanation for being abroad during the waiting period.
